note.explanation: Metal atoms release some outer electrons. These electrons move freely among positively charged metal ions and attract them, holding the metal together.
examples: In sodium, each atom releases one electron.
In magnesium, each atom releases two electrons, so its metallic bond is stronger than sodium's.
note.checkAnswer: Mobile electrons hold positively charged metal ions together.
note.simple: Imagine positive metal ions surrounded by a shared pool of moving electrons. The attraction between them holds the metal together.
note.checkQuestion: What holds the positive ions together in a metallic bond?
note.title: Metallic Bond
steps: Metal atoms lose their outer electrons easily.
The released electrons move freely between the metal ions.
The mobile electrons attract the positively charged ions and bind them together.
The mobile electrons also help metals conduct heat and electricity.
note.answer: A metallic bond is the attraction between positively charged metal ions and mobile electrons.

steps.text: Each sodium atom sets free one electron, but each magnesium atom releases two electrons.

steps.why: The strength of a metallic bond depends partly on the number of mobile electrons released by each atom.
steps.text: The magnesium ions have two positive charges and are associated with more mobile electrons.

steps.why: More positive charge and more mobile electrons make the metallic bond in magnesium stronger than that in sodium.
steps.text: Therefore, the metallic bond in magnesium is stronger than the metallic bond in sodium.

example.question: Why does magnesium melt at a higher temperature than sodium?
example.answer: Magnesium releases two electrons per atom, so its metallic bond is stronger than sodium's, which melts at a lower temperature.

explain.title: What is a metallic bond?
explain.body: Your textbook defines it this way: “A metallic bond, is therefore a type of chemical bond which has positively charged ions bound together by the mobile electrons.” Metal atoms release outer electrons easily. The electrons move freely among the positive ions and attract them together.

explain.title: What makes a metallic bond stronger?
explain.body: Its strength depends on the number of positive charges on the positive ions and the number of mobile electrons set free by each atom. Magnesium releases two electrons per atom, while sodium releases one, so magnesium has the stronger metallic bond.

explain.title: Why do metals conduct?
explain.body: Freely moving electrons in metals make them good conductors of heat and electricity.

explain.title: Why can metals change shape?
explain.body: Metal atoms are arranged in rows. When pressure is applied, the upper rows can slip past the lower rows, changing the metal's shape. Metals can therefore be drawn into wires and sheets.

explain.title: Other properties of metals
explain.body: Metals usually show metallic lustre, have high melting and boiling points, and are usually hard and heavy. Strongly held atoms arranged in rows help explain their hardness and heaviness.

mistakes: Do not say that the electrons stay attached to one particular metal nucleus; the section says they move freely and are shared collectively.
Do not define a metallic bond as a bond between positive and negative ions; that is not the section's definition.
Do not confuse the role of mobile electrons: they help explain conductivity, while rows of atoms slipping explain how metals change shape.
When comparing sodium and magnesium, remember that magnesium releases two electrons per atom and has the stronger metallic bond.
In an explanation of malleability or ductility, state that pressure makes rows of atoms slip past one another.
